title: Insurers: general claims handling duty (prompt and fair)
principle: An insurer must handle claims promptly and fairly, give the policyholder reasonable guidance and progress information, not unreasonably reject a claim (including by avoiding or terminating the policy) and settle promptly once terms are agreed. The duty is framed around the policyholder; a third-party claimant can cite it as leverage in a DISP complaint but it does not open the FOS to them (see DISP 2.7).
text: An insurer must: (1) handle claims promptly and fairly; (2) provide reasonable guidance to help a policyholder make a claim and appropriate information on its progress; (3) not unreasonably reject a claim (including by terminating or avoiding a policy); and (4) settle claims promptly once settlement terms are agreed.

title: Motor vehicle liability insurers: application of ICOBS 8.2 (answers BLUEPRINT §10 open question)
principle: On the text as returned, ICOBS 8.2 applies to every motor vehicle liability insurer (a firm with permission for motor vehicle liability insurance business). Only the rules about appointing claims representatives are confined to UK events/risks covered by a firm operating from an EEA establishment. The three-month reasoned offer/reply rule (8.2.6R) and the interest rules (8.2.9R–8.2.11R) carry no territorial limitation, and the Glossary "injured party" is any UK or EEA resident entitled to compensation for loss or injury caused by vehicles. So a purely domestic third-party claim against a UK-authorised insurer appears to be inside 8.2. Templates may rely on this only after a human has read the rule on the page.
text: (1) This section applies to a motor vehicle liability insurer. (2) The rules in this section relating to the appointment of claims representatives apply in relation to claims arising out of events occurring, and risks situated, in the United Kingdom, and covered by a firm operating from an establishment in the European Economic Area.

title: Reasoned offer or reasoned reply within three months of the claim
principle: Within three months of the injured party presenting a claim the at-fault driver's insurer must make a reasoned offer (liability not contested and damages quantified) or a reasoned reply to the points made (liability denied/unclear or damages not fully quantified). This is the ICOBS clock the system starts at NCAF; it is an FCA rule, not a GTA term, so it applies to non-subscribers.
text: Within three months of the injured party presenting a claim for compensation, the firm of the person who caused the accident (or its claims representative) must make a reasoned offer of compensation where liability is not contested and damages are quantified, or a reasoned reply where liability is denied or unclear or damages are not fully quantified.

title: Offer within three months of a later admission of liability
principle: Where liability was first denied or not admitted, the insurer must make a reasoned offer within three months of any later admission, provided the claim is by then fully quantified. Log the admission date as a fresh three-month clock.
text: If liability is initially denied, or not admitted, within three months of any subsequent admission of liability, the firm must (directly, or through a claims representative) make a reasoned offer of settlement, if, by that time, the relevant claim for damages has been fully quantified.

title: When a claim is "fully quantified"
principle: The three-month offer duty bites only once the claim is fully quantified, which happens when the injured party supplies written evidence substantiating the amounts. Operationally: the payment pack (hire invoice, storage/recovery accounts, engineer's report, mitigation and need evidence) is what starts the quantified clock — send it early and record the date.
text: A claim for damages will be fully quantified for the purpose of this section when the injured party provides written evidence which substantiates or supports the amounts claimed.

title: Interest where no offer is made in time: Bank of England base rate + 4%
principle: If the insurer (or its claims representative) fails to make the required offer, it must pay simple interest on the compensation it later offers or the court awards, from the date the offer should have been made until payment, at Bank of England base rate plus 4%, unless a tribunal awards interest. Templates may claim this only as against a UK-authorised motor insurer and only once the three-month clock has run from a fully quantified claim.

title: Final response within eight weeks of receiving a complaint
principle: A respondent must, by the end of eight weeks from receipt of a complaint, send a final response (accept and offer redress, offer redress without accepting, or reject with reasons) or a holding response explaining the delay and telling the complainant they may now go to the FOS. The complainant then has six months from the final response to refer. The eight-week clock in the system starts on the date the complaint is received by the firm.

CCGUK itself (a micro-enterprise) is eligible against its own insurer or bank; eligibility still requires the DISP 2.7.6R relationship.

title: Relationship with the respondent — third-party motor claimants are generally NOT eligible against the at-fault insurer
principle: A complainant must have one of the listed relationships with the respondent: customer/potential customer, or for insurance a person for whose benefit the policy was taken out, or a person on whom the right to benefit from a claim under the policy has devolved by contract, assignment, subrogation or legislation — but expressly NOT via the European Communities (Rights against Insurers) Regulations 2002. That carve-out is the third-party RTA claimant's only route, so a claimant cannot take the at-fault insurer to the FOS (FORUM_NOT_OPEN). title: Claims management perimeter: the six kinds of claim — is motor damage / credit hire recovery inside?
principle: Regulated claims management activity (FSMA s.22(1B); RAO arts 89G–89M) is seeking out/referring/identifying claims, or advising, investigating or representing a claimant, by way of business in Great Britain, in relation to six kinds of claim only: personal injury; financial services or financial product; housing disrepair; specified benefit; criminal injury; employment-related — subject to the exclusions in arts 89N–89W. A tort claim for vehicle damage, hire, storage and recovery against the at-fault driver (met by that driver's insurer) is not one of the listed kinds on the face of the list, which is why motor damage/credit hire recovery is generally understood to sit OUTSIDE the perimeter. Two traps: (a) any personal-injury element brings referral and advice inside arts 89G/89H (refer out, no fee — LASPO ss.56–60); (b) a claim or complaint by a policyholder against THEIR OWN insurer under their own policy is a claim in relation to a regulated activity (effecting/carrying out contracts of insurance) and so a "financial services or financial product claim" — advising on or representing a client in a FOS complaint against their own insurer for a fee is likely inside art 89I. Take regulatory advice before offering that service; do not assume an exclusion.

citation: FSMA 2000 (Regulated Activities) Order 2001, SI 2001/544, arts 89G–89M (inserted by SI 2018/1253)
title: Specified claims management activities and the kinds of claim they cover
principle: Art 89G: seeking out, referrals and identification of claims or potential claims (seeking out persons who may have a claim; referring details of a claim/claimant to another person; identifying a claim or claimant) when carried on in relation to a personal injury, financial services or financial product, housing disrepair, specified benefit, criminal injury or employment-related claim. Arts 89H–89M: advising a claimant, investigating a claim or representing a claimant in relation to each of those six kinds respectively (89H personal injury; 89I financial services/product; 89J housing disrepair; 89K specified benefit; 89L criminal injury; 89M employment-related). "Personal injury claim" takes the CPR meaning (damages for or arising from personal injuries). Exclusions follow in arts 89N–89W (e.g. legal professionals, charities, persons with insurance-distribution permissions acting in relation to a contract of insurance).
